java.title: Java
java.description: A beginner-to-intermediate introduction to Java, from setup and core syntax through object-oriented programming.

modules.title: Setup and first program
modules.description: Understand the Java development kit, source files, compilation, and the entry point of a program.
notes: Install a Java Development Kit (JDK), which includes the compiler javac and the java runtime launcher. Check an installation with java --version and javac --version.
Java source is saved in a .java file. javac compiles source into bytecode in a .class file, and java runs that class on the Java Virtual Machine.
A basic application starts in public static void main(String[] args). Java is case-sensitive, and statements generally end with semicolons.
takeaways: Save this example as Main.java because the public class is named Main.
Compile with javac Main.java, then run with java Main.
System.out.println prints a line of text.

modules.title: Types and variables
modules.description: Declare values using Java's primitive types and reference types, and use expressions with compatible types.
notes: A variable declaration gives a value a name and type, for example int count = 3. Java checks types at compile time; incompatible assignments must be converted explicitly when appropriate.
Common primitive types include int for whole numbers, double for decimal values, boolean for true or false, and char for one UTF-16 code unit. String is a reference type, not a primitive.
Use final for a local variable that should not be reassigned. Descriptive names and clear numeric types make intent easier to understand.
takeaways: Choose a type that represents the value and operations you need.
String values can be combined with + for readable output.
A variable's declared type constrains which values it can hold.

modules.title: Conditions and loops
modules.description: Choose between branches and repeat work with for and while loops.
notes: An if/else statement selects a branch using a boolean condition. Relational operators include <, <=, ==, and !=; use && and || to combine boolean conditions.
A for loop is useful when the number of iterations is known or controlled by a counter. A while loop repeats while its condition remains true.
Update loop state so the condition eventually becomes false. Braces group multiple statements and help make control flow clear.
takeaways: The remainder operator % can test divisibility, as in n % 2 == 0.
A for loop combines initialization, continuation condition, and update.
Use braces for predictable, readable branching and looping.

modules.title: Arrays and strings
modules.description: Store fixed-size sequences in arrays and work with immutable text using String methods.
notes: An array has a fixed length and stores elements of one declared type. Its first index is 0, and its final valid index is length - 1.
The enhanced for loop visits each element when its index is not needed. Accessing an invalid index causes an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
String objects are immutable: methods such as toUpperCase return a new string rather than modifying the original. Use equals to compare string contents.
takeaways: Array indices start at zero and array length is fixed after creation.
Prefer enhanced for loops when you only need each element.
Compare strings with equals rather than == when checking text content.

modules.title: Methods and parameters
modules.description: Organize logic into reusable methods with explicit parameters and return types.
notes: A method signature includes its name and parameter types; its declaration also specifies a return type. Use void when a method does not return a value.
Arguments are passed to parameters when a method is called. Java passes values by value, including a copy of a reference when the argument is an object reference.
Methods can be overloaded by using the same name with different parameter lists. A return statement provides a result and exits the method.
takeaways: Give each method one clear responsibility and a descriptive name.
The declared return type must match the value returned.
static methods can be called from main without creating an object.

modules.title: Classes and objects
modules.description: Model data and behavior together with classes, constructors, fields, and instance methods.
notes: A class defines a type; an object is an instance of that class. Fields store object state, and methods implement behavior.
A constructor initializes a new object and has the same name as the class with no return type. The new keyword creates an instance.
Encapsulation keeps fields private and exposes intentional operations through methods. The this keyword refers to the current instance.
takeaways: Constructors establish valid initial object state.
Private fields protect implementation details from direct outside changes.
Create objects with new and use their public methods to request behavior.

c.title: C
c.description: Learn the foundations of C, including compilation, control flow, arrays, pointers, structures, and files.

modules.title: C basics and compilation
modules.description: Write a small C program and compile it into an executable.
notes: C is a compiled language. Save source in a .c file and compile it with a C compiler such as gcc, for example gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra main.c -o main.
The #include directive makes standard library declarations available. stdio.h declares input/output functions such as printf.
Execution begins at main. A return value of 0 conventionally reports successful completion to the operating system.
takeaways: Save the program as main.c and compile it before running it.
Include the standard header for the library functions you use.
Use int main(void) when the program takes no command-line arguments.

modules.title: Types, variables, and operators
modules.description: Represent values with C's basic types and form expressions with arithmetic and comparison operators.
notes: Declare a variable before use, such as int count = 4;. Common basic types include char, int, float, and double; exact integer ranges depend on the implementation.
Arithmetic operators include +, -, *, /, and %. Integer division discards the fractional part, while division involving a floating-point operand can retain a fraction.
Use meaningful initial values and format specifiers that match the values passed to printf, such as %d for int and %.1f for double.
takeaways: Declare variables with a type that suits their values.
Be mindful of integer division when calculating fractions.
Match each printf conversion specifier to the corresponding argument type.

modules.title: Branching and loops
modules.description: Use conditions to select behavior and loops to repeat a calculation.
notes: An if/else statement evaluates an expression as true or false; in C, zero is false and nonzero is true. Comparison operators include ==, !=, <, and >=.
A for loop groups initialization, a continuation condition, and an update. A while loop checks its condition before each iteration.
The break statement exits a loop, while continue skips to its next iteration. Use braces to make multi-statement blocks explicit.
takeaways: Use == to compare values and = to assign them; they are different operators.
A loop needs a condition and state update that allow it to finish.
The remainder operator is useful for checking even and odd integers.

modules.title: Arrays and strings
modules.description: Work with fixed-size arrays and null-terminated character strings safely.
notes: An array stores a fixed number of same-type elements contiguously. C does not automatically check array bounds, so loops must stay within valid indices 0 through length - 1.
A C string is a char array ending with the null character '\0'. Reserve space for that terminator as well as the visible characters.
Use standard string functions such as strlen from string.h to inspect strings. Avoid unbounded input functions; this example uses known, bounded literals.
takeaways: C arrays do not carry bounds checks; track their length carefully.
Every C string needs room for its terminating null character.
Use size_t for sizes and indices returned by standard size-related functions.

modules.title: Functions and pointers
modules.description: Split programs into functions and use pointers to refer to objects when indirect access is needed.
notes: A function prototype declares a function's name, return type, and parameter types before use. Keep declarations and definitions consistent.
A pointer stores an address. The address-of operator & obtains an object's address, and the dereference operator * accesses the object at a valid pointer.
C passes function arguments by value. Passing a pointer lets a function modify the caller's object; only dereference pointers that point to valid objects.
takeaways: Use functions to give reusable operations clear inputs and outputs.
Use & to pass an object's address and * to access the pointed-to object.
Never dereference an uninitialized or otherwise invalid pointer.

modules.title: Structures and files
modules.description: Group related data in structures and perform basic file output with checked resources.
notes: A struct defines a composite type whose fields can have different types. Access a structure variable's fields with the dot operator.
The standard I/O library represents an open file with FILE *. fopen returns NULL if opening fails; check the result before using it.
Check write operations when reliability matters, and close successfully opened files with fclose. This example writes a fixed, harmless line to a local file.
modules.output:
Wrote C Basics (3 credits)
Creates course.txt containing: C Basics: 3 credits
takeaways: Use structures to group values that describe one entity.
Check fopen before reading from or writing to a file.
Close every successfully opened file and handle possible write failures.

cpp.title: C++
cpp.description: Build C++ skills from basic syntax through functions, standard containers, classes, and the STL.

modules.title: C++ basics and output
modules.description: Compile a small C++ program and use the standard output stream.
notes: C++ source files commonly use .cpp. A compiler such as g++ can build a program with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra main.cpp -o main.
Include standard library headers for the facilities used. The iostream header provides std::cout and std::endl or the newline character for output.
Execution begins at main. Returning 0 signals successful completion; using std:: names makes library identifiers explicit.
takeaways: Save the source as main.cpp and compile it with a C++ compiler.
Use std::cout with the insertion operator << to print output.
C++ programs conventionally return 0 from main on success.

modules.title: Types, variables, and control flow
modules.description: Use typed variables and conditionals and loops to express decisions and repetition.
notes: C++ has built-in types such as int, double, char, and bool, as well as library types such as std::string. Initialize variables when declaring them.
Use const when a value should not be modified through that name. Type deduction with auto is useful when the initializer makes the intended type clear.
if/else selects a path based on a condition, while loops repeat statements. A for loop is commonly used for a known sequence of iterations.
takeaways: Initialize variables and use const to communicate fixed values.
C++ uses == for comparison and = for assignment.
Loop conditions and updates should make progress toward termination.

modules.title: Functions and references
modules.description: Define reusable functions and pass values by reference when a function should work with an existing object.
notes: A function declaration states its return type and parameter types; a definition provides its body. Put a declaration before a call when the definition appears later.
A reference is an alias for an existing object and must be initialized. A non-const reference can modify its referent; a const reference is useful for efficient read-only access.
Pass small built-in types by value when a copy is simple. References avoid copying larger objects and can express intended modification.
takeaways: A function parameter declared T& can modify the caller's object.
Use const T& for read-only access to larger objects without copying.
Give functions clear return types and parameter contracts.

modules.title: Vectors and strings
modules.description: Use standard library containers for resizable sequences and text rather than managing raw arrays unnecessarily.
notes: std::vector<T> stores a resizable sequence of elements of type T. Its size() reports the number of elements; valid indices range from zero to size() - 1.
A range-based for loop visits elements without explicit index arithmetic. Use references in the loop when modifying elements, or const references for read-only access.
std::string represents text and provides methods such as size(). Include vector and string headers to use these types.
takeaways: Prefer std::vector for a resizable collection of same-type values.
Use range-based for loops when direct indexed access is unnecessary.
Use std::string for ordinary text instead of manually managed character buffers.

modules.title: Classes and encapsulation
modules.description: Define a class that holds private state and exposes a small, useful public interface.
notes: A class combines data members and member functions. Members declared private are accessible only through the class's own permitted operations.
A constructor initializes an object and can use a member initializer list. The public section defines operations available to callers.
Create an object by declaring a variable of the class type. Member functions can read or update the object's state while preserving its invariants.
takeaways: Keep implementation state private and provide purposeful public methods.
Use initializer lists to initialize members in constructors.
Mark read-only member functions const so they promise not to modify object state.

modules.title: The STL: algorithms and iterators
modules.description: Use standard algorithms with container iterators to express common operations clearly.
notes: The Standard Template Library (STL) provides containers, iterators, and algorithms. Include the specific headers needed, such as algorithm and numeric.
std::sort rearranges a range specified by its beginning and end iterators. For a vector, begin() and end() describe the half-open range containing all elements.
std::accumulate in numeric computes a fold such as a sum. Algorithms work with ranges, helping separate the operation from the underlying container.
takeaways: Use established standard algorithms instead of rewriting common loops.
Iterator ranges conventionally include the first iterator and exclude the last.
Include the standard header that declares each library feature you use.

javascript.title: JavaScript
javascript.description: Learn JavaScript from language basics through functions, collections, and browser DOM events.

modules.title: JavaScript basics
modules.description: Run a first JavaScript program and understand statements, expressions, and console output.
notes: JavaScript can run in a browser or in a server-side runtime such as Node.js. A .js file can be run with node main.js when Node.js is installed.
Use console.log to write diagnostic or learning output. Semicolons are often optional because of automatic semicolon insertion, but consistent style helps avoid ambiguity.
JavaScript is case-sensitive and executes statements in order. Comments can document intent without changing program behavior.
modules.code: console.log("Hello, JavaScript!");
takeaways: Save the example as a .js file and run it with Node.js, or paste it into a browser console.
Use console.log to inspect values while learning and debugging.
Capitalization matters in JavaScript identifiers.

modules.title: Variables and types
modules.description: Declare variables with let and const and recognize JavaScript's common value types.
notes: Use const for bindings that will not be reassigned and let for bindings that will. Avoid var in new code because its function-scoped behavior can be surprising.

JavaScript is dynamically typed: a binding can hold values of different types over time. Common values include number, string, boolean, undefined, and objects; null represents an intentional absence of an object value.

Template literals use backticks and ${expression} for readable string interpolation. typeof can help inspect many primitive values, though typeof null is the historical exception and returns "object".
modules.output:
3 notebooks in stock: true
number string
takeaways: Prefer const by default and use let when reassignment is necessary.
JavaScript values have types even though variables are not declared with fixed types.
Template literals interpolate values using ${...}.

modules.title: Operators and control flow
modules.description: Combine expressions, make decisions, and repeat operations using JavaScript operators and loops.
notes: Arithmetic operators include +, -, *, /, and %. The + operator adds numbers or concatenates strings depending on its operands, so explicit conversions can prevent confusion.
Use === and !== for strict equality in most cases; they compare without coercing differing types. Logical operators include &&, ||, and !.
if/else selects a path, and for or while repeats work. A loop should update its state so its condition eventually becomes false.
takeaways: Prefer strict equality (===) to avoid implicit type coercion surprises.
Use conditionals to select behavior and loops to repeat a bounded operation.
The remainder operator can test whether a number is divisible by two.

modules.title: Functions
modules.description: Create reusable functions using declarations, parameters, and return values.
notes: A function declaration names a reusable block of code and specifies parameters in parentheses. Call it with arguments to supply values for those parameters.
return sends a value back to the caller and ends that function invocation. If no return value is specified, the result is undefined.
Arrow functions offer concise syntax and are commonly assigned to const bindings. They also use lexical this, which differs from this in some traditional function calls.
takeaways: Use parameters to make a function work with different inputs.
Return a result when the caller needs to use the computation.
Keep functions focused and name them according to their purpose.

modules.title: Arrays and objects
modules.description: Represent ordered collections with arrays and related named data with objects.
notes: Arrays are ordered collections with zero-based indices. Common methods include push to add to the end and map to create a new array by transforming each element.
Objects store properties as key-value pairs. Dot notation accesses a property when its name is known, while bracket notation supports dynamic property names.
const prevents reassignment of the array or object binding, but it does not make the contained object or array immutable. Avoid mutating shared data unintentionally.
takeaways: Use arrays for ordered sequences and objects for named properties.
map returns a transformed array without changing the original array.
A const object binding can still refer to an object whose properties are mutable.

modules.title: DOM and events
modules.description: Connect JavaScript to a web page by selecting elements and responding to user events.
notes: The Document Object Model (DOM) represents a page as objects. Methods such as document.querySelector select elements using CSS selectors; check that a selection succeeded before using it.
addEventListener registers a callback for an event such as click. The callback runs when the event occurs, keeping interaction logic separate from markup.
textContent sets or reads plain text safely. Avoid inserting untrusted strings with innerHTML, which interprets content as markup.
modules.code: Ready
modules.output:
Before clicking: Ready
After clicking Greet: Hello from the page!
takeaways: Use querySelector to find page elements and account for a missing match.
Register event handlers with addEventListener instead of embedding interaction code in markup.
Use textContent for plain user-visible text rather than interpreting strings as HTML.
